{{lowercase title}}
In [[mathematics]], for <math>k \in \mathbb{N}</math>, a '''<math>k</math>-graph''' (also known as a '''higher-rank graph''' or '''graph of rank <math>k</math>''') is a [[countable]] [[category (mathematics)|category]] <math>\Lambda</math> together with a [[functor]] <math>d : \Lambda \to \mathbb{N}^k</math>, called the '''degree map''', which satisfy the following [[factorization]] property: 

<blockquote> if <math>\lambda \in \Lambda </math> and <math> m,n \in \mathbb{N}^k </math> are such that <math> d(\lambda) = m + n </math>, then there exist ''unique'' <math>\mu,\nu \in \Lambda</math> such that <math>d( \mu ) = m </math>, <math> d( \nu ) = n</math>, and <math>\lambda = \mu\nu </math>. </blockquote>

An immediate consequence of the factorization property is that morphisms in a <math>k</math>-graph can be factored in multiple ways: there are also unique <math>\mu',\nu' \in \Lambda</math> such that <math>d( \mu' ) = m </math>, <math> d( \nu' ) = n</math>, and <math> \mu \nu = \lambda = \nu' \mu' </math>. 

A 1-graph is just the [[path category]] of a [[directed graph]]. In this case the degree map takes a path to its length. 
By extension, <math>k</math>-graphs can be considered higher-dimensional analogs of directed graphs.

Another way to think about a <math>k</math>-graph is as a [[edge coloring|<math>k</math>-colored directed graph]] together with additional information to record the factorization property. 
The <math>k</math>-colored graph underlying a <math>k</math>-graph is referred to as its '''skeleton'''.  
Two <math>k</math>-graphs can have the same skeleton but different factorization rules. 

Kumjian and Pask originally introduced <math>k</math>-graphs as a generalization of a construction of Robertson and Steger.<ref>{{citation |first1=A.|last1=Kumjian |first2=D.A. |last2=Pask |title=''Higher rank graph C*-algebras'' |journal=[[The New York Journal of Mathematics]] | volume=6 |pages=1–20 | year=2000 |url=http://nyjm.albany.edu/j/2000/6-1.html}}</ref> By considering representations of <math>k</math>-graphs as bounded operators on [[Hilbert space]], they have since become a tool for constructing interesting [[C*-algebra]]s whose structure reflects the factorization rules. Some [[compact quantum group|compact quantum groups]] like <math>SU_q(3)</math> can be realised as the <math>C^*</math>-algebras of <math>k</math>-graphs.<ref>{{cite arXiv |mode=cs2 |first1=O.|last1=Giselsson |title=Quantum SU(3) as the C*-algebra of a 2-Graph | year = 2023|class=math.OA |eprint=2307.12878}}</ref>
There is also a close relationship between <math>k</math>-graphs and [[Factorization system|strict factorization systems]] in [[category theory]].


== Notation ==
The notation for <math>k</math>-graphs is borrowed extensively from the corresponding notation for categories:

* For <math>n \in \mathbb{N}^k</math> let <math>\Lambda^n = d^{-1} (n)</math>. By the factorisation property it follows that <math>\Lambda^0 = \operatorname{Obj} ( \Lambda )</math>.

* There are maps <math> s : \Lambda \to \Lambda^0</math> and <math> r : \Lambda \to \Lambda^0</math> which take a morphism <math> \lambda \in \Lambda </math> to its '''source''' <math> s(\lambda)</math> and its '''range''' <math> r(\lambda)</math>.

*For <math>v,w \in \Lambda^0</math> and <math>X \subseteq \Lambda</math> we have <math>v X = \{ \lambda \in X : r ( \lambda ) = v \}</math>, <math>X w = \{ \lambda \in X : s ( \lambda ) = w \}</math> and <math> v X w = v X \cap X w</math>.

* If <math>0 < \# v \Lambda^n < \infty</math> for all <math>v \in \Lambda^0</math> and <math>n \in \mathbb{N}^k</math> then <math>\Lambda</math> is said to be row-finite with no sources.

== Skeletons ==
A <math>k</math>-graph <math>\Lambda</math> can be visualized via its skeleton. Let <math>e_1 , \ldots , e_n</math> be the canonical
generators for <math>\mathbb{N}^k</math>. The idea is to think of morphisms in <math>  \Lambda^{e_i} = d^{-1}(e_i)</math> as being edges in a directed graph of a color indexed by <math>i</math>.

To be more precise, the '''skeleton''' of a  <math>k</math>-graph <math>\Lambda</math> is a [[edge coloring|''k''-colored directed graph]] <math>E=(E^0,E^1,r,s,c)</math> with vertices
<math>E^0 = \Lambda^0</math>, edges <math>E^1 = \cup_{i=1}^k \Lambda^{e_i}</math>, range and source maps inherited
from <math>\Lambda</math>,
and a color map <math> c: E^1 \to \{ 1 , \ldots , k \}</math> defined by <math>c (e) = i</math>
[[if and only if]] <math>e \in \Lambda^{e_i}</math>.

The skeleton of a <math>k</math>-graph alone is not enough to recover the <math>k</math>-graph. The extra information about factorization can be encoded in a complete and associative collection of [[commutative diagram|commuting squares]].<ref>{{citation |first1=A.|last1=Sims |title=''Lecture notes on higher-rank graphs and their C*-algebras''|url=https://www.aidansims.com/files/k-graphNotes2010.pdf}}</ref> In particular, for each <math>i \ne j</math> and <math> e,f \in E^1</math> with <math>c(e) = i</math> and <math>c(f) = j</math>, there must exist unique <math>e',f' \in E^1</math> with <math>c(e') = i</math>, <math>c(f') = j</math>, and <math>ef = f'e'</math> in <math>\Lambda</math>. A different choice of commuting squares can yield a distinct <math>k</math>-graph with the same skeleton.

== Examples ==
* A 1-graph is precisely the path category of a directed graph. If <math> \lambda</math> is a path in the directed graph, then <math>d(\lambda)</math> is its length. The factorization condition is trivial:  if <math> \lambda </math> is a path of length <math>m+n</math> then let <math> \mu </math> be the initial subpath of length <math>m</math> and let <math> \nu </math> be the final subpath of length <math> n </math>. 

* The [[monoid]] <math>\mathbb{N}^k</math> can be considered as a category with one object. The identity on <math>\mathbb{N}^k</math> give a degree map making <math>\mathbb{N}^k</math> into a <math>k</math>-graph.

* Let <math>\Omega_k = \{ (m,n) : m,n \in \mathbb{Z}^k , m \le n \}</math>. Then <math>\Omega_k</math> is a category with range map <math>r(m,n)=(m,m)</math>, source map <math>s(m,n)=(n,n)</math>, and composition <math>(m,n)(n,p)=(m,p)</math>. Setting <math>d(m,n) = n-m</math> gives a degree map. The factorization rule is given as follows: if <math>d(m,n) = p + q</math> for some <math>p,q \in \mathbb{N}^k </math>, then <math>(m,n) = (m,m+q) (m+q, n)</math> is the unique factorization.

== C*-algebras of k-graphs ==
Just as a [[graph C*-algebra]] can be associated to a directed graph, a universal C*-algebra can be associated to a <math>k</math>-graph.

Let <math>\Lambda</math> be a row-finite <math>k</math>-graph with no sources then a '''Cuntz–Krieger <math>\Lambda</math>-family''' or a '''represenentaion of <math>\Lambda</math>''' in a [[C*-algebra]] ''B'' is a map <math>S \colon \Lambda \to B</math> such that
# <math> \{ S_v : v \in \Lambda^0 \}</math> is a collection of mutually orthogonal [[projection (linear algebra)|projections]];
#  <math>S_\lambda S_\mu = S_{\lambda \mu}</math> for all <math>\lambda,\mu  \in \Lambda</math> with <math>s(\lambda) =r(\mu) </math>;
# <math> S_\mu^* S_\mu = S_{s ( \mu )}</math> for all <math> \mu \in \Lambda </math>; and
# <math>S_v = \sum_{\lambda \in v \Lambda^n} S_\lambda S_\lambda^*</math> for all <math>n \in \mathbb{N}^k</math> and <math>v \in \Lambda^0.</math>

The algebra <math>C^* ( \Lambda )</math> is the [[universal property|universal]] C*-algebra generated by a Cuntz–Krieger <math>\Lambda</math>-family.
